clinical_knowledge.topic: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes prompt histologic confirmation, full staging with PET-CT, and initiation of curative-intent R-CHOP chemoimmunotherapy given the aggressive but chemosensitive nature of this lymphoma, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: rapidly enlarging painless neck mass, drenching sweats, and weight loss
Key HPI features: 60M presenting with rapidly growing 5cm cervical lymph node mass, fevers, and night sweats. Biopsy confirms aggressive CD20+ diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.1C, HR 92, BP 126/78, unintentional weight loss of 8kg over 2 months. Firm, non-tender, rubbery 5cm right cervical lymph node; no other palpable lymphadenopathy; no hepatosplenomegaly on exam. Bloods: mild normocytic anemia, LDH markedly elevated (poor prognostic marker), ESR elevated. Excisional lymph node biopsy with immunohistochemistry confirms CD20-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Hodgkin lymphoma without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapid growth over weeks — this pace is itself a warning sign of an aggressive lymphoma.
management_principles: Complete staging workup: whole-body PET-CT, bone marrow biopsy, LDH, and HIV/Hepatitis B and C serologies (Hepatitis B screening is essential before Rituximab due to reactivation risk)
Obtain baseline echocardiogram (LVEF) before anthracycline-containing chemotherapy
Initiate curative-intent R-CHOP chemoimmunotherapy (Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide, Doxorubicin, Vincristine, Prednisone) every 21 days for 6 cycles
Give tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis (allopurinol and IV hydration) before the first cycle given the tumor's rapid proliferation rate
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.assessment: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL), an aggressive but potentially curable non-Hodgkin lymphoma, presenting with a rapidly enlarging cervical mass and B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss).
reference_soap.plan: 1. Complete staging workup: whole-body PET-CT, bone marrow biopsy, LDH, and HIV/Hepatitis B and C serologies before starting Rituximab. 2. Obtain baseline echocardiogram (LVEF) given planned anthracycline (doxorubicin) exposure. 3. Initiate curative-intent R-CHOP chemoimmunotherapy (Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide, Doxorubicin, Vincristine, Prednisone) every 21 days for 6 cycles. 4. Give tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis (allopurinol and IV hydration) before cycle 1 given the tumor's rapid proliferation rate. 5. Urgent referral to hematology-oncology; counsel patient on the aggressive-but-curable nature of DLBCL and expected treatment course.

teaching.one_liner: The most common aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma, presenting as a rapidly enlarging lymph node mass with B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) — fast-growing but often curable with chemotherapy.
red_flags: Rapid growth over weeks — this pace is itself a warning sign of an aggressive lymphoma

must_ask.say: How quickly has this lump grown — over weeks?
Have you had fevers, drenching night sweats, or weight loss?
Where is the lump, and is it painful?
When did you first notice it?
Any fatigue or loss of appetite?
